clue.text: Royal flush?

parts.note: not the poker hand but a king with a red face: the Norman king nicknamed 'the Red' for his ruddy complexion

explanation.surface: A card player lays down the best hand in poker.
explanation.walkthrough: The poker hand is the false trail. Read 'Royal flush' as a flushed (red-faced) royal: William II of England was called Rufus, Latin for red.
explanation.definitionFit: William II was nicknamed Rufus, Latin for 'red', supposedly for his ruddy face, so he is a monarch with a permanent flush.

clue.text: One is boxed in, truth to tell

definitions.text: One is boxed in, truth to tell

parts.words: One is boxed in, truth to tell
parts.note: a person who stands in a courtroom box to give truthful evidence

explanation.surface: Someone admits frankly to feeling trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Truth to tell' reads as 'frankly'; it is the job of the person in the court's witness box, sworn to tell the truth.
explanation.definitionFit: In court the person giving evidence stands in a box and swears to tell the truth.

clue.text: The Heavies that hold the Lights

definitions.text: The Heavies that hold the Lights

parts.words: The Heavies that hold the Lights
parts.note: heavy metal strips that hold the small panes in a leaded window, also read as lead actors holding the limelight

explanation.surface: Big stars of the stage hog the spotlight.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre is the false trail: the heavy metal strips hold the panes ('lights') of a window, and leads are also the principal actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Strips of lead metal hold the panes of a leaded window, and principal actors are the leads.

clue.text: Combine in get-up to charge

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' tells the solver to read the word before it from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
to rate is to charge or price at a given rate

explanation.surface: Putting on an outfit and charging ahead together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get-up' looks like an outfit, but 'up' reverses GET to TEG in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To integrate is to merge parts into a whole, to unite or blend.

clue.text: Medieval damp-course ?

parts.note: a damp-course keeps a wall dry; here it is a water-filled ditch round a castle, a course of damp

explanation.surface: Asking about building damp-proofing in the Middle Ages.
explanation.walkthrough: A damp-course is a waterproof layer in a wall; read as 'damp course', it is a channel of water round a castle.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval castle was surrounded by a deep water-filled ditch for defence.

clue.text: Far from friendly relations in Lundy, oddly enough

indicators.note: the relations are placed within the letters of the island's name
'oddly' says the island's name is set out in an odd new order

parts.note: kin are one's relations

explanation.surface: Family members on Lundy turn out to be curiously unfriendly.
explanation.walkthrough: Lundy is a small island in the Bristol Channel, off the coast of Devon. 'In' and 'oddly enough' both look like part of the surface remark, but they are the container and anagram signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting unkindly is the opposite of acting in a kind, friendly way.

clue.text: Bare the head? Silence a toy pistol ?

definitions.meaning: to take off one's hat or cap
a cap gun fires small explosive caps; taking them out leaves it silent

explanation.definitionFit: Removing a cap can mean doffing headgear or removing the percussion cap from a toy gun so it cannot bang.

clue.text: Sort of plain why shoes lose their shape

definitions.meaning: a flat stretch of country without woods, like a steppe
shoes kept without shoe trees, the wooden forms put in them, lose their shape

explanation.definitionFit: A plain with no woods is bare of trees, and shoes left without shoe trees inside them go out of shape.

clue.text: Follower of Chesterton's man and of 19

definitions.meaning: G. K. Chesterton wrote 'The Man Who Was Thursday', and the day after Thursday follows him

explanation.definitionFit: The day after Thursday, the title day of Chesterton's novel, shares its name with Robinson Crusoe's servant.

clue.text: That after-dinner speech torture—-at breakfast too!

definitions.text: That after-dinner speech torture—-at breakfast too!

parts.note: a toast is a short speech proposing a health after dinner
the rack was an instrument of torture

explanation.surface: Enduring a boring after-dinner speech is agony, and now it follows you to breakfast too.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines as well: the speech and the torture together make the holder that stands on the breakfast table.
explanation.definitionFit: A rack is a frame holding slices of toast upright on the breakfast table.

clue.text: Dr. Salter

definitions.meaning: a doctor heals illness, so is one who restores to health
one who salts meat or fish preserves it, the sense of curing bacon

explanation.definitionFit: A doctor heals the sick and a salter preserves meat with salt; both make things better in the two senses of the verb to cure.

clue.text: Junior officer on the staff

definitions.meaning: formerly the lowest commissioned infantry officer, who carried the colours; also a junior US naval officer
a flag flown on a flagstaff

explanation.definitionFit: The rank once held by a young infantry officer carrying the regimental colours is also the name for a flag flying from a pole.

clue.text: Stone-breaker's baccy? It grows wild

parts.note: to knap is to break stones or flints with a hammer, so that is the stone-breaker's word
tobacco is familiarly called 'the weed'

explanation.surface: A quarryman smokes a rough tobacco that might as well be growing wild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baccy' is informal British for tobacco, often called the weed.
explanation.definitionFit: Knapweed is a wild plant of the daisy family, a common meadow and roadside flower.

clue.text: His queen is a piece of cake !

definitions.text: His queen is a piece of cake !

parts.words: His queen is a piece of cake !
parts.note: the wife of an Eastern ruler takes the same title as a dried grape found in fruit cake

explanation.surface: A man whose wife is easy to manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A piece of cake' suggests something easy; here it is a literal ingredient. The ruler's wife is a sultana, also the name of a seedless raisin baked into cakes.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruler of a Muslim state has a wife titled sultana, which is also a kind of raisin.

clue.text: The stay of the fielding side?

definitions.text: The stay of the fielding side?

parts.words: The stay of the fielding side?
parts.note: a cricket fielder placed far behind the wicketkeeper to stop balls

explanation.surface: A cricket team in the field finds its innings dragging on.
explanation.walkthrough: Long stop is a cricket fielding position behind the wicketkeeper, a last line of defence; 'stay' means support as well as a stop.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the fielder stationed far behind the wicketkeeper backs up the keeper and stops balls that pass him.

clue.text: The known style of a dedication, said Johnson

definitions.text: The known style of a dedication, said Johnson

parts.words: The known style of a dedication, said Johnson
parts.note: Samuel Johnson's view of a book's dedication to a patron: fulsome, insincere praise

explanation.surface: Dr Johnson remarks on how book dedications are usually written.
explanation.walkthrough: Dedications to patrons in Johnson's day were notorious for excessive praise, and Johnson himself was sardonic about them.
explanation.definitionFit: A dedication to a wealthy patron was typically full of excessive, insincere praise in hope of reward.

clue.text: Two sailors with two articles that are trumpeted

parts.note: a tar is a sailor, the first of the pair
an is the indefinite article, the first of the pair
the second tar, another word for a sailor
a is the other indefinite article

explanation.surface: Two seamen accompany a couple of items that are announced with fanfare.
explanation.walkthrough: The sailors and articles alternate: TAR, AN, TAR, A.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarantara imitates the sound of a trumpet or bugle call, so it names notes blown on one.

clue.text: Play Peter ? Plead for Jingle ? Causes black looks

parts.note: to beg is to plead
rimes, an old spelling of rhymes, are jingles of verse

explanation.surface: Theatrical instructions to act a part and plead, then angry glances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play Peter' gives the answer another way: BE GRIMES, play Peter Grimes, the fisherman of Britten's opera. 'Black looks' are scowls but also a sooty face.
explanation.definitionFit: To begrime is to make dirty with soot, so it gives someone a blackened appearance.

clue.text: Like Easter paraders, or others in the park

definitions.text: Like Easter paraders, or others in the park

parts.words: Like Easter paraders, or others in the park
parts.note: people in an Easter parade wear decorated hats, and the 'others in the park' are cars in a car park with their engine covers

explanation.surface: Easter crowds stroll through the park in their finery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Others in the park' looks like more strollers; it means cars in a car park, which have bonnets (British for the hood over the engine).
explanation.definitionFit: Easter paraders wear Easter hats and parked cars have engine hoods, both called bonnets in British English.

clue.text: It packs a punch

parts.note: the upper-arm muscle that provides the force behind a blow

explanation.surface: Something strong and forceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Packs a punch' sounds like praise for a strong drink; literally, this arm muscle supplies a punch's power.
explanation.definitionFit: The large muscle at the front of the upper arm flexes to deliver the power of a blow.

clue.text: Robinson's jar clearly differed from the widow's

definitions.text: Robinson's jar clearly differed from the widow's

parts.words: Robinson's jar clearly differed from the widow's
parts.note: the widow's jar is the biblical cruse of oil that never ran dry; Robinson's surname is the same jar word with an O, nothing, in it

explanation.surface: Comparing two neighbours' storage jars and noticing one is different.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1 Kings 17 the widow's cruse (small jar) of oil never emptied. Robinson's name is CRUSE with O (zero, empty) inside, so his jar is the opposite of hers.
explanation.definitionFit: Robinson Crusoe is Defoe's castaway, so this is Robinson's surname.

clue.text: How a conductor's ground down ?

parts.note: an electrical conductor connected to the ground, and a hunted fox run to its burrow

explanation.surface: An orchestra conductor ends up worn down.
explanation.walkthrough: The orchestra is the false trail: an electrical conductor joined to the ground is earthed, and a fox chased into its burrow (earth) is earthed too.
explanation.definitionFit: An electrical conductor is earthed when wired to the ground for safety; 'ground down' reads as sent down into the ground.

clue.text: The wool makes money, nothing more

parts.note: cash is ready money
mere means nothing more than, as in 'a mere child'

explanation.surface: A dealer explains that fine wool earns money and that is all.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is the fine soft wool of the Kashmir goat.

clue.text: Civil Service dress

parts.note: not civil servants' uniform but the civilian clothes worn by a serviceman off duty

explanation.surface: The dress code for government office workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civil Service' looks like the government's administrative staff; read it as 'civil' dress for a member of the armed services.
explanation.definitionFit: Mufti is plain civilian clothing worn by someone who normally wears uniform.

clue.text: Learnt maybe to wear velvet

indicators.note: 'maybe' says the letters of the word before it might appear in another arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone who has learnt that they should dress in velvet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' turns LEARNT into the new word. A deer's growing horn is covered in soft skin called velvet, so the definition describes what that horn does.
explanation.definitionFit: A deer's new horn grows covered in a furry skin called velvet, which is later rubbed off.

clue.text: 1 dn, must not counsel, but a ship may

definitions.text: 1 dn, must not counsel, but a ship may

parts.words: 1 dn, must not counsel, but a ship may
parts.note: a person giving evidence must not deceive the barrister, while a ship can stop with its head to the wind

explanation.surface: A rule that applies to people in court but not to vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 down is WITNESS: a witness must not lie to counsel (a barrister); a ship lies to when it stops, head to wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship lies to when it holds still with its head into the wind; a witness may not tell untruths to the court.

clue.text: Firm relationship

parts.note: the abbreviation for brothers seen in company names, such as Warner

explanation.surface: A strong, steady bond between two people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' reads as steadfast; it is a business, whose name may end with the abbreviation for brothers, a family relationship.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation for brothers appears in many company names, so it marks a family tie within a business.

clue.text: The reading of a galley-slave ?

parts.note: not a rower chained to an oar but a printer's or editor's checking of type set in a galley tray

explanation.surface: Wondering what a chained oarsman on a galley might read.
explanation.walkthrough: In printing, a galley is the tray of set type and a galley proof is the first print taken from it for checking; the 'galley-slave' is the person reading it.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial impression of typeset text, taken from the galley tray, is read and corrected before final printing.

clue.text: A profligate in like case to Moreton in Morocco

indicators.note: the profligate is placed inside, as Moreton is 'in' its marsh

parts.note: the Gloucestershire town is Moreton-in-Marsh, so the case it is in is a marsh
a rake is a dissolute, profligate man

explanation.surface: A dissolute man finds himself in the same situation in Morocco as a Cotswold town.
explanation.walkthrough: Moreton-in-Marsh is a market town in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, England; the rake sits in a MARSH the way Moreton does. The opening 'A' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Marrakesh is a major city in Morocco.

clue.text: Titled chief of Fleet

parts.note: the professional head of the Royal Navy, whose title names him a lord of the Admiralty

explanation.surface: A nobleman heads a fleet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' might suggest Fleet Street and a newspaper chief; it is the navy. The title is that of the Royal Navy's senior officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The senior naval officer on the Admiralty Board, professional head of the Royal Navy, holds this title.
